questions.q: In the Cypher pattern (p:Person)-[:WORKS_AT]->(c:Company), what does the square-bracket portion represent?
options: A relationship of type WORKS_AT, with the arrow showing the direction it's stored in
A second node labeled WORKS_AT
A SQL JOIN condition written in Cypher syntax
A comment describing the query's purpose
questions.explain: Relationships are written in square brackets on a dash; the arrowhead shows the direction the relationship is stored in the graph.

questions.q: Which Cypher clause is the closest conceptual analog to a SQL SELECT list?
options: RETURN
MATCH
CREATE
MERGE
questions.explain: RETURN decides which nodes, relationships, or properties come back as results — the same role a SELECT list plays in SQL.

questions.q: Per this lesson, why is traversing a relationship like -[:WORKS_AT]-> fundamentally cheaper than computing an equivalent SQL Server JOIN on large tables?
options: The relationship is a stored physical record with direct pointers to its two nodes, so traversal is a constant-time lookup regardless of overall database size
Neo4j secretly builds a temporary index before every query, just like SQL Server does
Cypher relationships are actually computed the same way SQL joins are — there's no real difference
Relationships in Neo4j are cached in memory permanently, which is why they're fast
questions.explain: A SQL JOIN is computed at query time and its cost scales with table size; a Cypher relationship is a stored pointer, so traversal cost doesn't grow with the size of the database.

questions.q: What happens when you write RETURN p on a matched node p, without specifying individual properties?
options: The entire node object comes back, including every property on it
Cypher throws a syntax error because a property list is required
Only the node's internal ID is returned
Only the node's label is returned
questions.explain: Unlike a relational SELECT, RETURN p returns the whole node object with all of its properties — Cypher doesn't require a fixed column list.

questions.q: What does omitting the arrowhead, writing -[:WORKS_AT]- instead of -[:WORKS_AT]->, do in a MATCH pattern?
options: Matches the relationship regardless of which direction it was stored in
Deletes the direction information from the underlying relationship permanently
Causes a syntax error, since every relationship must specify a direction
Reverses the stored direction of the relationship
questions.explain: Every relationship is stored with a direction, but a query can match it in either direction by leaving the arrowhead off.
